# Tenancy law and possession recovery

Long-term letting: lease terms, rent control, and how long it takes to recover
possession from a non-paying tenant. Sources in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## The trap, handled first

The research brief warned that Spain's widely circulated **20.5-month** figure is
squatting-specific (*okupación*) and must never be presented as a tenant
non-payment eviction duration.

**That figure does not appear anywhere in this run's fetched corpus.** A search
across all 204 fetched files, 157 of which carry text, for `20,5 mes`, `20.5 month`, `okupa` and `ocupación
ilegal` found only the CGPJ press note [31], and what that contains is not a
duration. It is a **caseload count**: 460 squatting-possession filings under art.
250.1.4º LEC in Q1 2026, down 22.3%. Filings, not durations; squatting, not
arrears.

The trap did not propagate. It is recorded here so that a future reader who
encounters 20.5 months elsewhere knows it was checked and rejected.

## Eviction duration for ordinary non-payment

The brief's priority was a duration attributed to a **named body**. One country
delivers it.

| Country | Non-payment eviction duration | Body | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **France** | **8-month incompressible minimum**; "often closer to two years" in practice | CNCJ, citing Sénat *Rapport n° 278 (2022-2023)* p. 46 | [30] |
| Spain | **Counts only.** 2,600 LAU evictions executed in Q1 2026 | CGPJ | [31] |
| Portugal | **Statutory deadlines only**, no observed duration | BAS / DGAJ | [34][35] |
| Italy | Counts only, and the official series was inaccessible | Ministero dell'Interno | — |
| Panama | Procedure only — and it is **administrative, not judicial** | MIVIOT | [36] |
| Costa Rica, Mexico, Hungary, Greece | **Nothing** | — | — |

### France — the only real number

The Chambre nationale des commissaires de justice, the statutory body whose
officers actually execute evictions, published 2025 figures on 17 March 2026
[30]:

> "il existe hors trêve hivernale, un délai minimal incompressible de **8 mois**
> entre le premier impayé et l'expulsion avec concours de la force publique.
> Dans la pratique, la durée réelle d'une procédure complète est souvent **plus
> proche de deux ans**"

**Attribution matters here.** The 8-month minimum is not CNCJ's own measurement —
CNCJ attributes it to the Sénat commission des lois, *Rapport n° 278
(2022-2023)*, p. 46, which was not retrieved. The "closer to two years" figure is
CNCJ's practitioner estimate, not a statistic. Court listing delays run "de
quelques semaines dans les petites juridictions à **8 à 10 mois** dans les
grandes métropoles", and CNCJ estimates only about **15%** of arrears notices end
in eviction.

2025 volumes, CNCJ's own first-party counts [30]: 175,000 *commandements de
payer* (+2.4%), 147,000 *assignations* (+1.3%), 59,200 judgments served (+30.4%),
80,600 orders to quit (−1.5%), 63,700 requests for police assistance (−0.7%), and
**30,500 executed evictions (+27.2%, from 24,000)**.

Procedural instability: the loi Kasbarian of 27 July 2023 cut the
notice-to-summons interval from two months to six weeks, but a Cour de cassation
*avis* of 13 June 2024 held it non-retroactive, so **two regimes now coexist**
depending on whether the lease predates 29 July 2023 [30].

### Spain — counts, and a subtitle error worth not repeating

CGPJ Q1 2026 [31]: 4,005 evictions executed in total (−45.4% year on year), of
which **2,600 derived from the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos** — 64.9% of the
total, down 53.9%.

The press note's own subtitle conflates share-of-total with year-on-year change,
writing "un 64,9 % menos lanzamientos por impago de alquiler". The body figures
are the correct ones and were arithmetically verified: 2,600 + 971 + 434 = 4,005;
2,600 ÷ 4,005 = 64.9%. Anyone citing this source should quote the body, not the
subtitle.

**No Spanish duration figure exists in this corpus.** The LAU itself was never
fetched, so the minimum term, notice periods and deposit cap are also absent.

### Portugal — a purpose-built fast-track, with statutory clocks

The *procedimento especial de despejo* runs electronically and exclusively
through the **Balcão do Arrendatário e do Senhorio**, a body under the DGAJ with
national competence [34]. Grounds include resolution for arrears. The court fee
is **€25.50** where the procedure value is ≤€30,000 and €51 above, the value
being 2.5 years' rent plus arrears. Counsel is mandatory only for the tenant's
opposition.

**A correction the citation audit forced, and it matters.** An earlier draft of
this file set out a specific PED clock — 15 days to respond, hearing within 20
days, delivery within 30 — and a State rent-assumption mechanism under NRAU art.
15.º-LA, attributing all of it to [35]. **None of those figures appears in the
[35] source text.** That source's own preamble places the substance in Lei 6/2006
(NRAU) arts. 15.º to 15.º-S, which was never fetched. The figures have been
removed rather than re-attributed, because this run has no source for them.

What [34] and [35] do support is the institutional shape: an electronic-only
procedure, exclusive national competence in the BAS, arrears as a ground, the
court fee, and the limited role of counsel. **The statutory timetable of the
Portuguese eviction procedure is a gap in this run**, not a finding.

No Portuguese performance statistic was retrieved either, so neither the
statutory clock nor the observed duration is available.

### Panama — possession recovery is administrative

MIVIOT's Dirección General de Arrendamientos handles eviction claims — "Demandas
de lanzamiento, lanzamiento por intruso, desahucio" — **at first and second
instance**, within the ministry rather than the ordinary courts [36]. It also
registers lease contracts, **holds the security deposit by consignment**, polices
illegal rent increases, and operates a **direct wage-deduction mechanism** for
rent. Provincial Housing Commissions operate under art. 57 of Ley 93 de 1973.

No durations, no deposit cap, no minimum term and no rent-increase limit are
stated; Ley 93 de 1973 itself was not retrieved.

## The cross-country proxy — and what it is not

The 2024 EU Justice Scoreboard quantitative factsheet, sourced from CEPEJ, gives
estimated time to resolve **litigious civil and commercial** cases at first
instance, 2022, in days [32]:

| Hungary | Portugal | France | Spain | Italy | Greece |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **134** | **238** | **333** | **359** | **540** | **746** |

Three caveats, all material:

1. **This is not an eviction duration.** It covers civil and commercial disputes
   generally. Presenting it as a possession-recovery time would misstate it.
2. **It is a calculated quantity**, not a measurement — pending cases ÷ resolved
   cases × 365 — indicating the minimum time a court would need at current
   throughput.
3. **The extraction carries a caveat.** These values came from a PDF chart where
   the country labels and the data row are separate lines. One analysis pass
   cross-validated every first-instance value against a second figure in the same
   document and found them consistent; a second pass noted the mapping was
   inferred from a strictly ascending series. The **ordinal ranking is safe**; the
   specific day counts should be re-verified against CEPEJ directly before being
   relied on. CEPEJ's own reports were inaccessible to this run [66].

It covers six of the nine. Costa Rica, Mexico and Panama have no equivalent.

The 2025 Scoreboard [33] adds only rank orders, its numeric values being images
that did not survive extraction. On companies' confidence that investments are
protected by law and courts, of 27 member states: France 10th, Italy 15th, Spain
18th, Hungary 19th, Portugal 20th, **Greece 26th**.

## Lease terms and rent control — Portugal is the only rich case

**Portugal** [21][10]:

- **Rent control on new leases.** Lei 56/2023 art. 34.º caps the initial rent of
  a new residential lease on a property let within the previous five years at the
  last rent "aplicado o coeficiente de **1,02**" — a **2% ceiling**. Missed
  statutory updates may be recovered via the NRAU art. 24 coefficients if no more
  than three years have passed; the 2023 coefficient is stated as **1,0543**.
  Deep remodelling attested by the municipality permits adding costs at up to
  **15% per year**.
- **A tax ladder that pays for longer leases.** CIRS art. 72 as amended sets a
  base autonomous rate of 25% on residential rental income, reduced by 10
  percentage points for leases of 5 to under 10 years, with a further 2 points per
  equal-length renewal capped at 10; 15 points for 10 to under 20 years; and 20
  points for 20 years or more. A further 5-point reduction applies where a new
  contract's rent is at least 5 points below the prior contract on the same
  property. Contracts signed from 1 January 2024 whose rent exceeds the
  per-typology limits by 50% are excluded, and early termination attributable to
  the landlord claws the reductions back retroactively with interest.
- **The accessible-rent regime (RSAA)**, annex iii to DL 97/2026: minimum term
  **three years**; rent ceiling set by portaria at **80% of the INE median rent
  for the concelho**; qualifying income **exempt from IRS and IRC**, conditional
  on uploading the contract to the IHRU platform by 15 January.

**Italy** [29]: electing cedolare secca means the landlord "rinuncia alla facoltà
di chiedere l'aggiornamento del canone di locazione… inclusa la variazione
accertata dall'Istat" — a waiver of all indexation for the contract's life. The
10% rate for *canone concordato* against 21% otherwise is a direct fiscal
incentive to accept controlled rent. **No Italian minimum term, notice period or
deposit cap is in this corpus** — Legge 431/1998 and the 4+4 / 3+2 structures
appear nowhere.

**France** [13][30]: statutory letting-fee ceilings per m² of *surface
habitable*, from 1 January 2026 — €12.10 very tight zone, €10.09 tight, €8.07
non-tight, €3.03 for the inventory — rising 0.87% and applying only to leases
signed from that date. Only four fee types may be charged to the tenant, split
half-and-half with the landlord, while **management fees fall entirely on the
landlord**. Rent regulation exists (*encadrement des loyers* under the loi Alur
as modified by the loi Élan) but **no cap percentages or IRL values were
retrieved**. From 1 January 2027 a decree of 12 February 2026 redefines rent
arrears as established once cumulative debt exceeds **€450** or three months'
non-payment, replacing the current 2× monthly rent test [30].

**Spain** [15]: the only tenancy-law content retrieved is a preamble note that
the LAU "no [hace] referencia a un plazo determinado" in distinguishing seasonal
from ordinary residential leases, relying on *causa* instead — which the drafters
concede has caused inspection difficulty. The LAU's own minimum term, notice and
deposit rules are not in this corpus.

**Greece, Hungary, Mexico, Costa Rica**: nothing. Not a minimum term, notice
period, deposit cap or rent-control rule for any of the four.

## Gaps

- Eviction duration for **eight of nine** countries.
- The Sénat report that is the actual origin of France's 8-month figure.
- Spain's LAU, Italy's Legge 431/1998, Portugal's base NRAU, Hungary's
  lakástörvény, Panama's Ley 93 de 1973, Costa Rica's Ley 7527, and Mexico's
  state civil codes — none retrieved.
- Italy's Ministry of the Interior *sfratti* series: the department page returned
  HTTP 403 and the one accessible news item reports 2014 data. The 2024 Italian
  eviction counts circulating in this corpus reach it second-hand via the French
  CNCJ document, whose own footnote points to an activist news outlet, not to the
  Ministry. They are not used in this study.
